text:
Ordering was deliberately left out of the Wolt plugin, and the user framed it as 'for now' rather than never.

Two reasons. The woltapi library's own README says the purchase path has never been tested with a real order: submit_prepared_order() only handles one restaurant, immediate home delivery and one saved card, and it is the call that actually charges you. Separately, this plugin is driven by an LLM, so any money-spending tool is one bad tool call away from a real charge.

If ordering is revisited, the library also lacks login, card enrollment, payment verification screens, scheduled orders, cancellation and refunds, and it needs browser/device information the caller has to supply itself. list_delivery_targets returns opaque IDs with no addresses, so a user cannot confirm where an order would go before submitting it.

The plugin also omits list_delivery_targets entirely for that same reason: opaque IDs are useless on their own.

Verified against 22 real checkout responses decoded from the woltapi HAR captures.

POST /order-xp/web/v2/pages/checkout returns the fee breakdown in checkout_rows, NOT in payment_breakdown. payment_breakdown splits the total across payment methods (total, unallocated, parts); with one card it carries no information, and unallocated was 0 in all 22 samples. checkout_rows is a list of rows keyed by a template field: amount_row holds the labelled fee lines, price_total_amount_row holds the displayed total. The row set is dynamic (Courier tip, Small order fee and Bottle deposits appear only sometimes) and labels embed data such as the delivery distance, so a label is never a stable key.

purchasing_disabled is present and null in all 22 samples. It is a nullable restriction, never a boolean, so testing 'is False' silently reports every valid basket as not allowed.

Do not trust the server's formatted_amount strings. In one response amount.formatted_amount was the euro-prefixed string while original_amount.formatted_amount for the same row lacked the symbol. Format from the integer cents instead.

Gotcha that cost real time: HAR response bodies are base64-encoded, with content.encoding set to base64. A search that json-parses content.text and swallows the error finds nothing and looks like proof that a field does not exist. Decode first.

A new compatible woltapi release does NOT reach the tools by itself. Each tool is a PEP 723 uv script, and uv caches the resolved environment per script. With the header pinned woltapi~=0.4.0, the tools kept running 0.4.0 after 0.4.1 was published, even though ~=0.4.0 permits 0.4.1 and 'uv tree --script' reported 0.4.1. 'uv run --refresh' did NOT dislodge it. Forcing 'uv run --with woltapi==0.4.1 ./run.py' proved the environment was the only difference.

This matters in production because the host spawns ./run.py through the '#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run' shebang and hits the same cache, so a library fix would silently never arrive.

The reliable fix is to bump the pin in all ten run.py headers, because changing the requirement string forces re-resolution. Treat the pin as the deployment mechanism, not just a compatibility range: after any woltapi release the plugin depends on, bump the pin to that exact minimum.

Debugging trap worth remembering: probing the version by copying run.py to another filename gives a DIFFERENT uv cache key, so the copy resolves fresh and reports the new version while the real script still serves the old one. The probe says everything is fine while the tool is broken.

woltapi 0.5.0 added delete_baskets(), which takes a list of basket IDs and can delete every saved basket in one call. The plugin deliberately does not expose that. empty_basket requires a slug and deletes only the baskets matching it.

The owner chose this when the tool was designed. The reason is blast radius: the tools are driven by an LLM, and a delete-everything parameter is one loose instruction away from wiping every saved basket, with no undo. Requiring a slug means a mistake costs one restaurant's basket.

Do not add a 'delete all' option or an optional slug without asking the owner first. The library supports it; the restraint is the plugin's, not the library's.

Also rejected at the same time: a 'clear' action inside update_basket. Every other action there requires an item_id, and a whole-basket action does not fit a tool whose contract is one item change.
